analysis.one_liner: Eliminates corporate tax deductions for executive pay above 100 times a firm's average employee wage.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors in May 2009, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2009 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the tax code so that companies could no longer deduct from their taxes the portion of any employee's pay that exceeds 100 times the average pay of their other employees. Pay counted broadly — salary, bonuses, stock options, retirement contributions, and benefits. Companies paying someone beyond that 100-to-1 line would pay taxes on the excess, and would have to report their lowest-paid, average, and top pay figures to the IRS.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because companies would either shrink top executive pay below the 100-to-1 threshold or pay more in taxes, reducing the tax burden everyone else shares. Workers whose employers tied executive compensation to the firm-wide average would see the gap between their pay and the CEO's narrowing become a tax consequence. Companies could still pay executives any amount; they would simply no longer get a tax deduction for the portion past 100 times the average.

how_it_helps.text: Denies corporations a tax deduction for the portion of any employee's pay above 100 times the company's average employee compensation [S2] [S3].
Counts all forms of pay — wages, bonuses, stock options, retirement contributions, and fringe benefits — so top earners cannot escape the cap by shifting compensation into options or benefits [S3].

Requires companies that pay anyone beyond the threshold to file a report with their lowest-paid, average, and highest-paid employee figures and the number of employees over the 100-to-1 line, creating a public record of pay gaps [S3].
Treats related companies as a single employer, preventing firms from splitting off a subsidiary with only executives to inflate the average [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations, and especially the financial and executive-heavy firms where top pay runs into the tens or hundreds of millions; they would lose deductions worth potentially hundreds of millions of dollars each, or would have to restructure executive pay. Publicly traded companies would also face new reporting on internal pay gaps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with highly paid executives

drawbacks.text: Compliance is complicated: employers must annualize the pay of part-time and part-year employees and calculate a firm-wide average across all forms of compensation, and companies with a few very low-paid workers could see their effective threshold drop sharply [S3].

A single firm with many low-paid employees would face a much lower dollar threshold than a firm with high average pay, so two companies with the same executive pay could face very different tax treatment [S3].
The deduction cap does not directly limit what executives are paid; a company could absorb the extra tax rather than narrow its pay gap, leaving pay inequality itself untouched [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is indirect but real: as long as executive pay is tax-deductible, ordinary taxpayers subsidize it, and this bill ends that subsidy past a 100-to-1 ratio while leaving companies free to pay whatever they choose. The main design weakness is that the threshold varies with each firm's own pay distribution, so the bill taxes some companies far more than others for similar executive pay, and it relies on firms choosing to cut pay rather than eat the tax. Even so, the cost falls on corporations with extreme pay gaps and the gain falls on the general taxpayer.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Finance Committee in June 2009, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on May 7, 2009; no other senator cosponsored it [S1] [S4].
It was first referred to the Banking Committee, which was discharged on June 2, 2009, and the bill was then referred to the Finance Committee, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — and the bill never received a Senate floor vote in the 111th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extremely highly paid executives kept their full tax deductions for that pay, since nothing was enacted; taxpayers at large saw no change either way.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations paying top executives; deductions stayed intact

for.name: Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois (Senate Majority Whip)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 7, 2009 and was its only sponsor; after Banking was discharged, the bill went to the Finance Committee he did not chair

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 2, 2009 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and only one senator, a Democrat, sponsored the bill with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever formed on the record.

industries.industry: Large corporations with highly paid executives
industries.note: The bill would end their tax deduction for pay above 100 times their firm's average employee compensation, a subsidy worth potentially hundreds of millions a year at the largest firms. Their gain in the actual outcome was the status quo: the deduction stayed intact because the bill died in committee.

industries.industry: Executive compensation consultants and pay benchmarking firms
industries.note: If enacted, firms restructuring pay around the 100-to-1 threshold would have needed extensive pay-structure advice, though the bill's death meant no new business materialized. Listed as the secondary beneficiary of the bill had it passed, not of the outcome.
